rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop and turns that discipline into three clean stories: pricing, operations, and labor. A's "Inside the kitchen where a robot halved the time it takes to make guac" is a real restaurant-ops angle; B's "Chipotle Is Running Two Kitchen Robots Simultaneously. Its Competitors Are Taking Notes." starts inventing market reaction before a reporter has a single competitor on record. B has useful bones, but it keeps putting a tuxedo on an inference and calling it a story.
gaps_in_A: "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices" still leans harder on causality than the update proves. The body flags the hole, but the headline sells the robot-price link before the math exists.

"whether the freeze covers all 3,500+ locations or only the 100 with Autocado" is slightly mis-aimed. The sharper issue is how a 100-store robot rollout could support a chainwide price pledge, not whether the pledge might only apply to robot stores.

"Inside the kitchen" assumes access and scene. Fine as an ambition, but the supplied facts only support a reported operations angle if Chipotle opens the pilot kitchen or provides real before/after numbers.
gaps_in_B: "Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" is invented. No competitor reaction appears in the update, and that phrase is exactly how a thin category angle starts pretending it has market proof.
"Labor Advocates Are Watching" is also an invented outside reaction. The angle can ask labor advocates to respond; it cannot claim they are already watching without evidence.

"Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" and "Robots Justify Flat Prices" are the same causal bet in different clothes. Split by consumer versus investor only works if you have actual margin math or analyst reaction.

"category-creation" and "layered approach to kitchen orchestration" are consultant fog. Digital Makeline is only in testing, with no scope or performance data, so it should be supporting detail until it earns its own story.
